title: Krylov Break Times from an Inhomogeneous Lieb--Robinson Light Cone
authors: Shunji Matsuura, Yoji Kawamura, Joseph Salfi, Satoshi Iso
abstract: Krylov and Lanczos approximations are used in quantum dynamics, quantum subspace methods, and Hamiltonian learning. A practical question is how long an $m$-dimensional Krylov truncation can be trusted. We argue that this time is fixed by causal propagation on the associated Jacobi chain. The relevant distance is not the Krylov index itself, but the inhomogeneous transport metric $ρ(m,n) = \sum_{j=\min(m,n)}^{\max(m,n)-1} 1/b_j$, where $b_j$ is the Lanczos hopping across the bond $j \leftrightarrow j+1$. We prove a Lieb--Robinson bound in this metric. Its small-weight limit gives the velocity $v_{\rm LR} = 2$, meaning that propagation is exponentially suppressed outside the cone $ρ(m,n) \simeq 2|t|$. The error of a finite Krylov approximation to the return amplitude is a round-trip effect: information has to travel from the probe to the truncation boundary and back. Combining the Lieb--Robinson bound with Duhamel's formula yields a lower bound on the error of the truncated dynamics. For a fixed tolerance $ε$, let the break time $t_\ast(m;ε)$ denote the longest time for which the $m$-dimensional truncation is guaranteed to reproduce the exact return amplitude within error $ε$. We show that $t_\ast(m;ε) \ge τ_m[1-o(1)]$, where $τ_m = ρ(0,m) = \sum_{j<m} 1/b_j$. When the probe spreads along the chain, this lower bound is also tight, so $t_\ast(m) \simeq τ_m$. The situation is different when the probe excites only a localized part of the spectrum, or a part already resolved by the truncation. In this case, essentially no signal reaches the boundary. Beyond a state-dependent Krylov dimension $m_\ast$, the approximation can therefore remain accurate at all times, and the break time is effectively infinite. Numerical tests on spin chains and random Jacobi matrices support $t_\ast(m) \simeq τ_m$ in the transport-limited regime.
summary: This theoretical work establishes a precise lower bound for the 'break time' of Krylov subspace approximations used to simulate quantum dynamics. The break time is found to be dictated by the inhomogeneous transport time scale ($	au_m$) derived from the system's underlying Jacobi chain structure. This result connects computational limitations directly to fundamental concepts like Lieb-Robinson bounds and causal propagation in quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental question of determining the reliable time window (break time) for using a finite-dimensional Krylov subspace approximation of quantum dynamics.
main_result: The break time $t^*(m; \epsilon)$ is shown to be lower-bounded by a characteristic transport time $	au_m = \sum 1/b_j$, suggesting that the approximation error is governed by the round-trip time scale.
method: The analysis combines the derivation of a Lieb-Robinson bound in an inhomogeneous transport metric with Duhamel's formula to establish a rigorous lower bound on the approximation error.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by a quantum Hamiltonian restricted to a Jacobi chain representation, which arises from the Lanczos recursion applied to an initial state $|v_0\rangle$. The dynamics are analyzed via the principal truncation $J_m$ of this matrix.
key_observables: Break time $t^*(m; \epsilon)$, Transport time $	au_m$, Lieb-Robinson velocity $v_{LR}$.
important_parameters: The error tolerance $\epsilon$, the dimension of the truncation $m$, and the local hopping parameters $b_j$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the structure of the Jacobi chain and assumes specific spectral properties (e.g., purely absolutely continuous spectrum) to establish the saturation of the lower bound.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the inhomogeneous transport metric, proving a Lieb-Robinson bound within this metric, deriving the lower bound on the break time using Duhamel's formula, and finally discussing the saturation of this bound under various spectral assumptions.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, physically motivated timescale ($	au_m$) for the breakdown of computationally intensive quantum simulation techniques (Krylov methods) when applied to spatially extended quantum systems.

Figure 2: One-way arrival and round-trip break time measure the same light cone. The red data show the endpoint arrival time tarr, defined by the first appearance of probability at the Krylov boundary. It scales as tarr/τm ≃1/2, as expected for one-way propagation with velocity 2. The blue data show the return-amplitude break time t∗, which scales as t∗/τm ≃1 because the boundary signal must travel out and back. The two slopes therefore support the same Lieb–Robinson velocity, not two different velocities.

Figure 3: Initial-state dependence of spectral capture. Left: the saturated amplitude error maxt |A(t) −Am(t)| ≈2ηm as a function of Krylov dimension m, for four initial states of the N = 8 XXZ ring (Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ), N´eel, domain wall, and a random broad- spectrum state). Each state resolves its spectral measure at a different rate, so the error drops below the tolerance ϵ (dashed line) at a different, state-dependent dimension m∗: a narrow-spectrum state such as GHZ is captured after only a few steps (m∗≈18), whereas a broad state stays uncaptured over the whole accessible range. Figure 5: Same transport slope for three models (single-site probe, N = 12, ϵ = 10−2): the XXZ ring, the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM, P j ZjZj+1 + P j Xj), and the mixed-field Ising model (MFIM, P j ZjZj+1 + 1.05 P j Xj + 0.5 P j Zj). After passing to the transport coordinate τm, all three collapse onto t∗≃τm; the model-dependent Lanczos plateaus are absorbed into the metric.
